text: In January 2021 US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) stopped a shipment of Uniqlo cotton shirts at the Port of Los Angeles/Long Beach under its order against cotton products of the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps (XPCC), issued on information that reasonably indicates forced labour. In a May 2021 ruling CBP held that Uniqlo had not shown the shirts were not made in part with forced labour and that they could not enter the US; CBP took the ruling off its website later that month.

source.name: U.S. Customs and Border Protection: ruling HQ H318182, Application for Further Review, Uniqlo Co., Ltd., XPCC Withhold Release Order (10 May 2021), text as archived by CustomsMobile
source.quote: The protestant has not established that the detained cotton garments were not produced in part by forced labor. Accordingly, the subject goods are inadmissible.

additionalSources.name: U.S. Customs and Border Protection: CBP Issues Detention Order on Cotton Products Made by Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps Using Prison Labor
additionalSources.quote: CBP’s Office of Trade directed the issuance of a Withhold Release Order (WRO) against cotton products made by the XPCC based on information that reasonably indicates the use of forced labor, including convict labor.

additionalSources.name: Bloomberg (Lisa Du), republished by The Japan Times: U.S. blocked Uniqlo shirts over Xinjiang forced-labor concerns
additionalSources.quote: customs agency blocked a shipment of Fast Retailing Co.’s Uniqlo shirts in January for violating an order prohibiting imports of items suspected to be produced by forced labor

additionalSources.name: International Trade Today (Warren Communications News): CBP Removes Recent Uniqlo Forced Labor Rulings
additionalSources.quote: CBP pulled down two recent rulings from its website that detailed the agency's detention of shipments imported by Uniqlo over suspected use of cotton from the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps in China.
